title: Identifying Gate Dependence and Bypass in Cancer
content: Targeted-therapy resistance is commonly interpreted in one of two ways: a tumour has become less dependent on the inhibited input, or it has acquired a parallel route to the same phenotype. Here, we argue that these explanations can be structurally indistinguishable when inference is based only on phenotype responses to manipulation of the inhibited gate. In a phenotype-first framework, each route requires route-specific cellular competence, execution drive, molecular context and reversible permissive gates; parallel routes sum before a phenotype-specific threshold is crossed. This formalism exposes an exact degeneracy between reduced gate dependence and additive bypass for a linear gate. The distinction becomes identifiable only when the architecture of the primary route is perturbed while the gate remains clamped. We outline the experimental designs needed to recover that distinction, test the multiplicative assumption itself and assess the predicted separation of recovery times. We also propose a prospective endocrine-resistance experiment, an assignment-reliability study and cross-cancer tests designed to prevent post hoc relabelling. The main implication is methodological: bypass should be treated as a structural claim that must be earned by a discriminating perturbation.
